title: Users That Actively Request Confirmation Messages
statement:
A service sends confirmation messages to the users who sign up:

- `Signups(user_id, time_stamp)`: one row per user with the datetime they signed up; `user_id` is unique.
- `Confirmations(user_id, time_stamp, action)`: one row per confirmation message a user requested, at datetime `time_stamp`. `(user_id, time_stamp)` is unique, every `user_id` appears in `Signups`, and `action` is `'confirmed'` or `'timeout'`.

Find the users who requested two confirmation messages **at most 24 hours apart**. Two requests exactly 24 hours apart count; 24 hours and one second apart do not. Only the request times matter, not the `action`. Return one column, `user_id`, listing each such user once. Rows may come in any order.
reference:
SELECT DISTINCT earlier.user_id
FROM Confirmations AS earlier
JOIN Confirmations AS later
  ON later.user_id = earlier.user_id
 AND later.time_stamp > earlier.time_stamp
WHERE TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, earlier.time_stamp, later.time_stamp) <= 24 * 60 * 60;
brute:
SELECT s.user_id
FROM Signups AS s
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM Confirmations AS a
  WHERE a.user_id = s.user_id
    AND EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM Confirmations AS b
      WHERE b.user_id = a.user_id
        AND b.time_stamp > a.time_stamp
        AND b.time_stamp <= DATE_ADD(a.time_stamp, INTERVAL 1 DAY)
    )
)
notes:
## Intuition

"Two requests at most 24 hours apart" is a statement about **pairs** of rows of the same user. Joining `Confirmations` to itself on `user_id` lists every pair; keeping only pairs where the second request is later avoids pairing a row with itself and counts each pair once. A pair qualifies when the gap between its two timestamps is at most 86,400 seconds, and a user qualifies when any of their pairs does.

## Approach

1. Take each request `earlier` and join it to every request `later` of the same user with a strictly later `time_stamp`.
2. Measure the gap with `TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, earlier.time_stamp, later.time_stamp)` and keep pairs at most `24 * 60 * 60` seconds apart (inclusive, so exactly one day counts).
3. `SELECT DISTINCT earlier.user_id`, because a user can have several qualifying pairs.

## Example 1, step by step

| user | earlier | later | gap (s) | kept |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | 2021-01-06 03:30:46 | 2021-01-06 03:37:45 | 419 | yes |
| 7 | 2021-06-12 11:57:29 | 2021-06-13 11:57:30 | 86401 | no |
| 2 | 2021-01-22 00:00:00 | 2021-01-23 00:00:00 | 86400 | yes |
| 6 | 2021-10-23 14:14:14 | 2021-10-24 14:14:13 | 86399 | yes |

Distinct users: 2, 3 and 6.

## Complexity

- Time: the self-join compares each request with the other requests of the same user, O(C + Σ kᵤ²) for C rows where user u has kᵤ requests; with an index on `(user_id, time_stamp)` this is close to O(C).
- Space: O(U) for the distinct users in the result.

## Pitfalls

- `TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, ...) <= 24` truncates: a gap of 24 hours 30 minutes reads as 24 hours and wrongly qualifies. Compare seconds.
- `< 86400` excludes the pair exactly one day apart, which must count.
- `DATEDIFF(...) <= 1` compares calendar days, so a request at 00:00 and another at 23:00 the next day (47 hours apart) would pass.
- Without `DISTINCT` a user with several close pairs appears several times.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `earlier` | one request of a user |
| `later` | another request of the same user with a later timestamp |
| `TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, ...)` | the gap between the two requests in seconds |
| `DISTINCT` | reports each qualifying user once |

narration.1: Report each user who owns at least one qualifying pair, once.
narration.2: Every confirmation request is a candidate first request of a pair.
narration.3: Join the table to itself so each request meets the other requests.
narration.4: Pairs are formed only within one user.
narration.5: Only later requests are paired, so no row pairs with itself and each pair appears once.
narration.6: Keep the pairs whose gap is at most 86,400 seconds; exactly one day still counts.
